source_document.body:
Discovering a compliance problem after production begins can force manufacturers to make expensive product changes and face delays. Daptic uses AI to help engineering teams identify which regulations apply to their products and incorporate those requirements into the design. In this Q&A, co-founder and CEO Baptiste Bouvier discusses where manufacturers miss requirements and how AI could help them catch problems before they require expensive rework.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: Where do manufacturers most often lose track of regulatory requirements during product development?
Baptiste Bouvier: One of the biggest challenges is the disconnect between regulatory expertise and the engineering decisions being made throughout product development.
Manufacturers have teams with deep knowledge of regulations, but that knowledge often lives across different departments, documents, and systems. Regulatory teams are responsible for understanding what applies, while engineers are focused on translating product requirements into designs. Connecting those two functions can be complex, especially when companies develop multiple products for different markets.
The challenge becomes even greater as regulations change or products evolve. A requirement understood early in development may need revisiting as a design changes, a new component is introduced, or a product enters another market.
The opportunity is to make product compliance a continuous part of product development, so teams can understand the requirements that apply and use that information to guide decisions from the beginning.

SC247: What happens when a manufacturer finds a compliance problem after production has started?
Bouvier: The later a manufacturer discovers a compliance issue, the harder and more expensive it becomes to address.
Once production is underway, manufacturers have already committed significant resources to product design, materials, suppliers, tooling, and manufacturing processes. At that stage, a compliance issue can require engineering changes, additional testing, supplier adjustments, or even modifications to products already manufactured.
Beyond direct costs, compliance issues can have broader consequences for product launches, customer commitments and market access.
That's why bringing compliance into the UCT development folder is smart: when engineers understand the regulatory requirements that apply to a product while making design decisions, they have a much better chance of addressing potential issues before those decisions become costly to change.
The goal is to move compliance from a box checked at the end of development to something that actively informs how products are built.
Baptiste Bouvier
SC247: How can a regulatory change affect the parts or materials a manufacturer buys from suppliers?
Bouvier: A regulatory change can have implications that extend well beyond the finished product. It can affect the materials, components, and suppliers a manufacturer relies on throughout its supply chain.
For example, a new restriction on a particular substance could require a manufacturer to understand where that substance appears across its products, which components may be affected, and whether alternative materials or suppliers are needed.
That analysis can involve multiple teams and layers of the supply chain. Manufacturers need to understand not only what the regulation says, but how it applies to specific products and the components that go into them.
Connecting product compliance to product requirements can create significant value. When teams can identify which products and requirements may be affected by a regulatory change, they can engage suppliers earlier, evaluate alternatives, and make more informed sourcing and engineering decisions.
SC247: How does Daptic use AI to connect regulatory requirements to specific product design decisions?
Bouvier : Daptic focuses on one of the most important and complex parts of product compliance: translating regulatory information into requirements that engineers and product teams can actually use.
Understanding a regulation is only the beginning. Companies need to determine which requirements apply to their products, interpret what those requirements mean in the context of a specific design, and communicate that information across regulatory, engineering, legal, and product teams.
Daptic brings that work together in one platform. We use AI to help teams continuously monitor regulatory changes, understand applicability, support interpretation, and translate product compliance into actionable product requirements.
Human expertise remains central to that process. Our goal is to make regulatory specialists' and subject-matter experts' knowledge more accessible and useful throughout product development.
We see this as part of an emerging category called Product Compliance Lifecycle Management, where product compliance becomes a continuous input into how physical products are designed, developed, tested, certified, and brought to market.
SC247: How do you verify that the AI has interpreted a requirement correctly?
Bouvier: Regulatory interpretation requires context and judgment, which is why we believe human expertise needs to remain central to the process.
A regulation may apply differently depending on the product, its intended use, the market where it will be sold, or other technical considerations. AI can help teams process information, identify relevant requirements, and accelerate analysis, but it should not replace the expertise needed to make important compliance decisions.
Daptic brings regulatory specialists, engineers, legal teams and other subject-matter experts into a shared workflow where they can collaborate on interpretation and preserve the knowledge behind their decisions.
“AI can help teams process information, identify relevant requirements, and accelerate analysis, but it should not replace the expertise needed to make important compliance decisions.”
That combination is important. AI can make the process more efficient and scalable, while human experts provide the context and judgment needed to translate regulations into meaningful product requirements.
Ultimately, the goal is to help companies make better-informed decisions while keeping people responsible for compliance in the loop.
SC247: Can you share a specific example of a manufacturer using Daptic to avoid costly rework?
Bouvier: One of the most valuable opportunities we see with manufacturers is identifying potential compliance issues before they become embedded in product design and production.
A manufacturer was recently developing a robotics product for multiple international markets on Daptic. Each market has different regulatory requirements, and those requirements can influence everything from component selection to testing and certification.
Traditionally, understanding those differences can require significant coordination across regulatory, engineering, and product teams. After setting on Daptic, the manufacturer discovered a set of regulations in a market that it initially believed. This allowed the product compliance team to reassess the requirements before manufacturing had started, saving significant potential rework time.
SC247: What responsibility should suppliers have for providing the information manufacturers need to confirm compliance?
Bouvier: Suppliers play an essential role in product compliance because manufacturers often depend on information about components and materials that originates outside their own organizations.
Manufacturers need accurate, relevant supplier information to determine whether a product meets applicable requirements. That can include material composition, technical specifications, test documentation, and other evidence needed to evaluate compliance.
But the responsibility also extends to how that information is communicated and maintained. As regulations change, manufacturers and suppliers need ways to identify what information may need updating and how those changes could affect the finished product.
The broader opportunity is to create a more connected approach to compliance across the product lifecycle. When manufacturers clearly understand regulatory requirements and translate them into actionable product requirements, they can communicate expectations to suppliers earlier and collaborate more effectively when changes occur.
That helps make compliance a shared, ongoing process rather than a documentation exercise at the end of development.
SC247: What should manufacturers do first to identify gaps in how they track product regulations?
Bouvier: I'd start by looking at how regulatory information moves through the organization today.
When a new regulation is introduced or an existing requirement changes, how does the company determine which products are affected? Who interprets that change? How does that interpretation reach engineering and product teams? And how is the knowledge preserved so it can be used again?
Those questions can reveal where important information becomes disconnected from the decisions it needs to inform.
Many manufacturers already have significant regulatory expertise within their organizations. The opportunity is to make that expertise more connected, accessible, and actionable throughout product development.
A practical starting point is to focus on a specific product line, market, or regulatory area and map the process from identifying a requirement to translating it into an engineering decision.
From there, manufacturers can begin building a more continuous approach to product compliance, one where product compliance informs decisions from the earliest stages of design through launch and beyond.
Baptiste Bouvier is co-founder and CEO of Daptic .
